newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU parliament offered veto in BSE row aftermath.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament offered veto in BSE row aftermath.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer, fighting to avoid censure for the way the Commission handled the mad cow crisis, on Tuesday offered the European Parliament the right of veto over European Union health policy.
The parliament should be given joint decision-making powers on health matters, Santer told a parliamentary debate.

The EU's complex "co-decision procedure", involving lengthy wrangling betweeen the parliament, the Commision and EU ministers, effectively gives the directly elected assembly a veto over legislation it does not like.
Santer said coordination of member states' health policies should be improved and where possible harmonised.
"Yesterday the Commission presented a concrete proposal to the (inter-governmental conference) IGC" currently revising the EU's Maastricht treaty, Santer said.
He said he would try to persuade the IGC, which is due to end in June, that all legislative decisions should be taken jointly.
"I hope they will have the courage to apply this principle to the CAP as well," Santer said, referring to the controversial and costly Common Agricultural Policy.

The parliament was debating a scathing report from its special committee of inquiry that attacks the Commission and Britain for making serious errors in the way they handled the outbreak of mad cow disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and trying to minimise the public health risk.
The crisis erupted in March 1996 when the British government admitted that BSE was linked to a deadly human equivalent.
